newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS - Banks wary on timing of Manila rate cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Banks wary on timing of Manila rate cut.

text.p: The Philippine central bank on Wednesday announced a four percentage point cut in its key overnight rate but banks remained concerned over the peso currency, which suffered de facto devaluation last week.

After the foreign exchange market closed, central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the overnight borrowing rate was being cut to 28 percent from the present 2-1/2 year high of 32 percent, effective Thursday.
The central bank decided to cut the rate after the currency market showed signs of normalisation, which led it to buy dollars again.
The rate was raised last week when the Philippine currency was under intense speculative attack.
"We don't know if the worst is over right now. There is still a lot of uncertainty in the market. We'll just have to wait and see," said Rafael Algarra, vice president of Standard Chartered Bank.
The central bank succumbed to the pressure last Friday when it allowed the peso to move in a wider range, which meant an effective devaluation.
In the two weeks before the decision to loosen its grip on the currency, the central bank spent nearly $2 billion to defend the peso.
It also raised interest rates to punitive levels, which had led to complaints from industry.
Though the lowering of interest rates was seen as a necessary move, analysts were not sure if the timing was right.
"We don't know whether it (the peso) will be subject to more pressure," said Banco Santander treasurer Antonio Agcaoili. "The overnight rate of 28 percent is, of course, a positive development.

"It's a natural consequence of this entire purpose of allowing the currency to float so they can lower interest rates and not defend the currency through monetary policy that would affect the credit markets," he said.
The high overnight rate had prompted some big banks to raise their prime lending rates above 30 percent this week.
However, bank officials said the effect of the peso's de facto devaluation, which could boost prices of fuel, power rates and basic commodities, might outweigh the impact of lower interest rates.
The peso had tumbled to a record low of 30 per dollar on Tuesday before recovering to 29/29.50 on Wednesday.
The central bank said it was confident that the peso could regain its strength by the end of the year.

"Our projection is that the average exchange rate for the third quarter of this year...will be between 27.00 and 28.00 pesos. In the last quarter, the average will be between 26 and 27," Singson said in an interview on government television late on Tuesday.
